newsitem.title: UK: Back-month UK rate futures offer value - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Back-month UK rate futures offer value - analysts.

text.p: Short sterling futures in 1998 and 1999 offer shrewd investors good value, even after hefty gains on Tuesday, following radical reforms to Britain's central bank, strategists said.

Two factors, they said, will conspire to drive contracts in 1998 and 1999 higher over the longer term -- the view they are discounting improbably large interest rate rises, and improved sentiment towards a European single currency under the new Labour government.

"As a rule of thumb, the combination of the domestic arugument that there's no need for base rates to go up as much as is discounted, and secondly the argument of a more friendly EMU government in power, means back month short sterling futures contracts offer value," said Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Markets here.

Short sterling contracts rose across the strip on Tuesday, even after a quarter-point interest rate rise and the announcment by Chancellor Gordon Brown of substantial moves towards Bank of England independence.
The back month contracts rose significantly more than the front month contracts -- as is usual in a whippy market.
The June 1997 contract was up 0.06 on the day at 93.41, while the June 1999 contract was up a hefty 22 basis points at 92.69.
This implies three month money rates around 7.30 percent by mid 1999 which would still imply another whole point rise in British interest rates over the next two years.

"We think base rates will peak at 6.5 percent by mid-summer, with any other policy response coming from the fiscal side," said Roberts. "So in that sense there is definitely value in the red contracts and some of the front month contracts."

Brian Venables, European bond strategist at ABN AMRO in Amsterdam, said he had revised his interest rate outlook up since the Bank will likely be more hawkish on rates than any government. He now expects rates of 6.75 percent by year end.
"That's taken some of the shine off the back months, but there's still clearly some value there," he said.
Analysts said a growing perception the new Labour government will be more receptive towards its European partners may also help boost back month short sterling contracts.

Brown reiterated on Tuesday that it was unlikely Britain would join a single European currency in 1999. But the markets nevertheless see Labour as more Euro-friendly than the previous Conservative administration.
Venables reported strong demand from Continental Europe for gilts and short sterling on Tuesday.
"Clearly Labour are going for a softer, less confrontational approach to Europe and that will have dividends for gilts and short sterling," he said.
"If there was any real liquidity in the 1999 back months, they would be a screaming buy."
